Split into five reusable obligations. The parent keeps only a three-line assembly.

The supplied proof has five separable layers:
(i) Step 1, measure theory: for a Lebesgue-null N, almost every translate x + w + R h of a line meets N in an L^1-null set (null envelope, Tonelli, translation invariance). This is segment_null = allard52_lad_segment_null.
(ii) Step 2(b)-(d), one-variable analysis: if phi is Lipschitz on [a,b] and its a.e. derivative is a continuous k, then phi(b) - phi(a) = integral_a^b k. This is lipschitz_ftc = allard52_lad_lipschitz_ftc. Mathlib's integral_deriv_eq_sub is real-valued only, and the R^l version needs the parent's phi - integral argument.
(iii) Step 3(b), parametric integrals: if U is open and convex and g is continuous on U, then (a,b) |-> integral_0^1 g(a + tau(b-a))(b-a) dtau is continuous on U x U (compact thickening plus dominated convergence). This is segment_integral_continuous = allard52_lad_segment_integral_continuousOn.
(iv) Steps 0, 2 and 3, the integral mean-value formula f(y) - f(x) = integral_0^1 g(x + tau(y-x))(y-x) dtau for x, y in an open convex U. This is line_integral_rep = allard52_lad_line_integral_rep, which depends on (i)-(iii).
(v) Step 4, Frechet differentiability at x from the formula and continuity of g. This is fderiv_of_line_integral = allard52_lad_hasFDerivAt_of_line_integral.

Step 3 removes the translation w. Here this is written as follows: F(w) = f(y+w) - f(x+w) - I(x+w, y+w) is continuous on B_rho(0) and a.e. zero, hence zero (Measure.eqOn_open_of_ae_eq). This is the parent's density-plus-continuity argument.

subproblems.title: Almost every parallel line meets a Lebesgue-null set in a null set
subproblems.statement: Let n >= 0, let N be a subset of R^n with Lebesgue (outer) measure L^n(N) = 0 (N need not be measurable), and let x, h ∈ R^n. Then for L^n-almost every w ∈ R^n, the set {t ∈ R : x + w + t h ∈ N} has one-dimensional Lebesgue (outer) measure 0.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n : ℕ) (N : Set (Rn n)), volume N = 0 → ∀ (x h : Rn n), ∀ᵐ w ∂(volume : Measure (Rn n)), volume {t : ℝ | x + w + t • h ∈ N} = 0
subproblems.natural_proof:
Notation. L^n is Lebesgue measure (volume) on R^n = EuclideanSpace R (Fin n). It is an additive Haar measure, so it is translation invariant and sigma-finite. L^1 is Lebesgue measure on R. Measures of sets that may not be measurable are outer measures.

1. Measurable null envelope. Since L^n(N) = 0, there is a measurable set N' with N ⊆ N' and L^n(N') = 0 (exists_measurable_superset_of_null).

2. The set E. Define Psi : R^n x R -> R^n by Psi(w, t) := x + w + t h. Psi is continuous: it adds a constant, the first projection, and the second projection times the fixed vector h. Hence Psi is measurable from the Borel sigma-algebra of R^n x R to the Borel sigma-algebra of R^n (Continuous.measurable). The Borel sigma-algebra of R^n x R is the product sigma-algebra, because both factors are second countable. Therefore E := Psi^(-1)(N') = {(w, t) : x + w + t h ∈ N'} is a measurable subset of R^n x R.

3. Every t-section of E is null. Fix t ∈ R. Since x + w + t h = w + (x + t h),
 {w ∈ R^n : (w, t) ∈ E} = {w : w + (x + t h) ∈ N'},
which is the preimage of N' under the translation w |-> w + (x + t h). Lebesgue measure is translation invariant (measure_preimage_add_right), so L^n({w : (w, t) ∈ E}) = L^n(N') = 0.

4. E is null for the product measure. E is measurable and L^n, L^1 are sigma-finite. Tonelli's theorem in the form Measure.prod_apply_symm gives
 (L^n x L^1)(E) = lintegral over t ∈ R of L^n({w : (w, t) ∈ E}) dL^1(t) = lintegral of 0 = 0.

5. Almost every w-section of E is null. Since E is measurable, Measure.measure_prod_null gives the equivalence: (L^n x L^1)(E) = 0 if and only if L^1({t : (w, t) ∈ E}) = 0 for L^n-a.e. w. Step 4 gives the left side. Hence L^1({t ∈ R : x + w + t h ∈ N'}) = 0 for L^n-almost every w.

6. Back to N. For each such w, {t : x + w + t h ∈ N} ⊆ {t : x + w + t h ∈ N'} because N ⊆ N'. Monotonicity of outer measure (measure_mono_null) then gives L^1({t : x + w + t h ∈ N}) = 0. This holds for L^n-almost every w ∈ R^n, which is the claim. The argument needs no assumption on n, x or h; for h = 0 it is unchanged.
proof_key_steps: Replace N by a measurable null superset N' (exists_measurable_superset_of_null)
E = {(w,t) : x + w + t h ∈ N'} is measurable, being the preimage under a continuous map
Each t-section of E is the translate N' - (x + t h), so it is L^n-null by translation invariance
Tonelli (Measure.prod_apply_symm): (L^n x L^1)(E) = 0
Measure.measure_prod_null: for a.e. w the section {t : x + w + t h ∈ N'} is L^1-null; monotonicity passes this to N

subproblems.title: Fundamental theorem of calculus for a Lipschitz curve with continuous a.e. derivative
subproblems.statement: Let l >= 0, phi, k : R -> R^l, a <= b real and L >= 0. Suppose phi is L-Lipschitz on [a, b], k is continuous on [a, b], and for Lebesgue-almost every t in the open interval (a, b) the map phi has derivative k(t) at t. Then phi(b) - phi(a) = integral_a^b k(t) dt.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (ℓ : ℕ) (φ k : ℝ → Rn ℓ) (a b : ℝ) (L : ℝ≥0), a ≤ b → LipschitzOnWith L φ (Icc a b) → ContinuousOn k (Icc a b) → (∀ᵐ t ∂(volume : Measure ℝ), t ∈ Ioo a b → HasDerivAt φ (k t) t) → φ b - φ a = ∫ t in a..b, k t
subproblems.natural_proof:
Notation. The integral from u to v is the oriented interval integral for Lebesgue measure on R. Since a <= b, [a, b] = Icc a b = uIcc a b.
Lean note: the absolute-continuity API used below is in Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Integral.IntervalIntegral.AbsolutelyContinuousFun. The frozen header does not import it, so add that import to the proof file.

1. Bound and integrability of k. k is continuous on the compact set [a, b], so there is C ∈ R with ||k(t)|| <= C for all t ∈ [a, b] (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn). For u, v ∈ [a, b], the closed interval between u and v lies in [a, b]. So k is continuous on it and therefore interval integrable on u..v (ContinuousOn.intervalIntegrable).

2. The primitive Psi(t) := integral_a^t k(s) ds is Lipschitz on [a, b]. Let u, v ∈ [a, b]. Step 1 gives integrability on a..u and a..v, so additivity of the interval integral (intervalIntegral.integral_interval_sub_left) gives Psi(u) - Psi(v) = integral_v^u k. Every s between v and u lies in [a, b], so ||k(s)|| <= C. By intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const,
 ||Psi(u) - Psi(v)|| <= C |u - v| <= C+ |u - v|, where C+ := max(C, 0) (Real.toNNReal C).
Hence Psi is C+-Lipschitz on [a, b] (LipschitzOnWith.of_dist_le_mul).

3. D := phi - Psi is absolutely continuous on [a, b]. phi is L-Lipschitz on [a, b] and Psi is C+-Lipschitz there. So D(t) = phi(t) - Psi(t) is (L + C+)-Lipschitz on [a, b] (LipschitzOnWith.sub, the additive form of LipschitzOnWith.div). A function that is Lipschitz on uIcc a b is absolutely continuous there (LipschitzOnWith.absolutelyContinuousOnInterval).

4. D has derivative 0 at almost every point of [a, b]. The endpoints a and b form an L^1-null set, so Ioo a b =ae Icc a b (Ioo_ae_eq_Icc). Combined with the hypothesis, for a.e. t: if t ∈ [a, b], then t ∈ (a, b) and phi has derivative k(t) at t. Fix such a t ∈ [a, b], so t ∈ (a, b).
 (i) k is continuous at t, since t is an interior point of [a, b] (Icc_mem_nhds) and k is continuous on [a, b].
 (ii) k is strongly measurable at the filter nhds t, since k is continuous on the open set (a, b) containing t (ContinuousOn.stronglyMeasurableAtFilter with isOpen_Ioo).
 (iii) k is interval integrable on a..t, by step 1 with a, t ∈ [a, b].
By the first fundamental theorem of calculus (intervalIntegral.integral_hasDerivAt_right), Psi has derivative k(t) at t. Therefore D = phi - Psi has derivative k(t) - k(t) = 0 at t (HasDerivAt.sub, then sub_self).

5. D is constant on [a, b]. Apply AbsolutelyContinuousOnInterval.const_of_ae_hasDerivAt_zero to D with the a.e. statement of step 4. This lemma holds for functions with values in any real normed space, in particular R^l. It gives a constant D0 with D(t) = D0 for all t ∈ uIcc a b = [a, b]. Both a and b lie in [a, b] because a <= b, so D(b) = D(a).

6. Conclusion. Psi(a) = integral_a^a k = 0, so D(a) = phi(a), and D(b) = phi(b) - Psi(b). Hence phi(b) - Psi(b) = phi(a), that is,
 phi(b) - phi(a) = Psi(b) = integral_a^b k(t) dt.
If a = b, both sides are 0 and the argument above covers this case unchanged.
proof_key_steps: k is bounded by C on [a,b] and interval integrable on every subinterval
The primitive Psi(t) = integral_a^t k is max(C,0)-Lipschitz on [a,b]
D = phi - Psi is Lipschitz, hence absolutely continuous on [a,b]
For a.e. t ∈ (a,b), phi' = k(t) by hypothesis and Psi' = k(t) by FTC-1, so D'(t) = 0; the endpoints are null
const_of_ae_hasDerivAt_zero: D is constant on [a,b]; with Psi(a) = 0, D(b) = D(a) gives the formula

subproblems.title: Continuity of the segment integral of a continuous operator field
subproblems.statement: Let n, l >= 0, let g : R^n -> L(R^n, R^l), and let U ⊆ R^n be open and convex with g continuous on U. Then the map I : R^n x R^n -> R^l, I(a, b) := integral_0^1 g(a + tau(b - a))(b - a) dtau, is continuous on U x U (product topology).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (g : Rn n → (Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ)) (U : Set (Rn n)), IsOpen U → Convex ℝ U → ContinuousOn g U → ContinuousOn (fun p : Rn n × Rn n => ∫ τ in (0:ℝ)..1, g (p.1 + τ • (p.2 - p.1)) (p.2 - p.1)) (U ×ˢ U)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Notation. L = L(R^n, R^l) carries the operator norm. R^n x R^n carries the product topology. I(a, b) := integral_0^1 g(a + tau(b - a))(b - a) dtau.

1. Segments stay in U. Let a, b ∈ U and tau ∈ [0, 1]. Then a + tau(b - a) = (1 - tau)a + tau b ∈ U by convexity, since 1 - tau >= 0, tau >= 0 and the coefficients sum to 1.

2. Reduction. Fix (a0, b0) ∈ U x U. It suffices to show that I is continuous at (a0, b0); then it is continuous within U x U at that point. Let S0 := {a0 + tau(b0 - a0) : tau ∈ [0, 1]}. S0 is compact, being a continuous image of [0, 1], and S0 ⊆ U by step 1.

3. A compact neighbourhood of the segment and a bound for g. S0 is compact, U is open and S0 ⊆ U. So there is delta > 0 such that the closed delta-thickening C := {z : dist(z, S0) <= delta} is contained in U (IsCompact.exists_cthickening_subset_open). C is compact because R^n is proper (IsCompact.cthickening). g is continuous on C ⊆ U, so there is M with ||g(z)|| <= M for all z ∈ C (IsCompact.exists_bound_of_continuousOn).

4. Nearby segments stay in C. Let W := {(a, b) : ||a - a0|| < delta and ||b - b0|| < delta}. It is a neighbourhood of (a0, b0), being the preimage of two open balls under the continuous projections. Let (a, b) ∈ W and tau ∈ [0, 1].
 (a + tau(b - a)) - (a0 + tau(b0 - a0)) = (1 - tau)(a - a0) + tau(b - b0).
Its norm is at most (1 - tau)||a - a0|| + tau||b - b0|| <= (1 - tau)delta + tau delta = delta. Since a0 + tau(b0 - a0) ∈ S0, the point a + tau(b - a) lies in C (mem_cthickening_of_dist_le). Also b - a = (b0 - a0) + (b - b0) - (a - a0), so ||b - a|| <= ||b0 - a0|| + 2 delta.

5. Dominated convergence. Put F((a, b), tau) := g(a + tau(b - a))(b - a) and use the constant bound B := M(||b0 - a0|| + 2 delta). We check the hypotheses of intervalIntegral.continuousAt_of_dominated_interval at (a0, b0) on the interval 0..1. Its set Ι 0 1 = (0, 1] is contained in [0, 1].
 (a) Measurability. Let (a, b) ∈ W. g is continuous on U, and tau |-> a + tau(b - a) is continuous and maps [0, 1] into C ⊆ U (step 4). So tau |-> g(a + tau(b - a)) is continuous on [0, 1]. Evaluating a continuous L-valued map at the fixed vector b - a keeps continuity (ContinuousOn.clm_apply). Hence tau |-> F((a, b), tau) is continuous on (0, 1]. It is therefore a.e.-strongly measurable for Lebesgue measure restricted to (0, 1] (ContinuousOn.aestronglyMeasurable, measurableSet_uIoc). This holds for every (a, b) in the neighbourhood W.
 (b) Domination. Let (a, b) ∈ W and tau ∈ (0, 1]. By ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm and steps 3-4,
 ||F((a, b), tau)|| <= ||g(a + tau(b - a))|| ||b - a|| <= M(||b0 - a0|| + 2 delta) = B.
Here M >= ||g(a + tau(b - a))|| >= 0.
 (c) The constant B is interval integrable on 0..1.
 (d) Continuity in the parameter. Fix tau ∈ (0, 1]. The point a0 + tau(b0 - a0) ∈ S0 ⊆ U lies in the open set U, so g is continuous at it (ContinuousOn.continuousAt with IsOpen.mem_nhds). The map (a, b) |-> a + tau(b - a) is continuous and sends (a0, b0) to that point. So (a, b) |-> g(a + tau(b - a)) is continuous at (a0, b0). The map (a, b) |-> b - a is continuous. Hence (a, b) |-> F((a, b), tau) is continuous at (a0, b0) (ContinuousAt.clm_apply).
So (a, b) |-> integral_0^1 F((a, b), tau) dtau = I(a, b) is continuous at (a0, b0).

6. Since (a0, b0) ∈ U x U was arbitrary, I is continuous on U x U. If U is empty there is nothing to prove.
proof_key_steps: Convexity: a + tau(b - a) ∈ U for a, b ∈ U and tau ∈ [0,1]
Fix (a0,b0): the segment S0 is compact in U, its closed delta-thickening C ⊆ U is compact, and ||g|| <= M on C
If ||a - a0||, ||b - b0|| < delta, every segment point lies in C and ||b - a|| <= ||b0 - a0|| + 2 delta

Dominated convergence (intervalIntegral.continuousAt_of_dominated_interval) with constant bound M(||b0 - a0|| + 2 delta): measurability from continuity in tau, pointwise continuity in (a,b) from continuity of g at points of the open set U

subproblems.title: Integral mean-value formula for a Lipschitz map with continuous a.e. derivative
subproblems.statement: Let n, l >= 0, f : R^n -> R^l, g : R^n -> L(R^n, R^l), U ⊆ R^n open and convex, and K >= 0. Suppose f is K-Lipschitz on U, g is continuous on U, and for Lebesgue-almost every x ∈ U the map f has Frechet derivative g(x) at x. Then for all x, y ∈ U: f(y) - f(x) = integral_0^1 g(x + tau(y - x))(y - x) dtau.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (f : Rn n → Rn ℓ) (g : Rn n → (Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ)) (U : Set (Rn n)) (K : ℝ≥0), IsOpen U → Convex ℝ U → LipschitzOnWith K f U → ContinuousOn g U → (∀ᵐ x ∂(volume : Measure (Rn n)), x ∈ U → HasFDerivAt f (g x) x) → ∀ x ∈ U, ∀ y ∈ U, f y - f x = ∫ τ in (0:ℝ)..1, g (x + τ • (y - x)) (y - x)
subproblems.natural_proof:
This is steps 0-3 of the parent proof, with an open convex set U in place of the ball B^o_r(c). It uses three sibling results:
 [segment_null] For every L^n-null N ⊆ R^n and x, h ∈ R^n: for L^n-a.e. w, L^1({t : x + w + t h ∈ N}) = 0.
 [lipschitz_ftc] Suppose a <= b, phi is Lipschitz on [a, b], k is continuous on [a, b], and phi has derivative k(t) at a.e. t ∈ (a, b). Then phi(b) - phi(a) = integral_a^b k.
 [segment_integral_continuous] If U is open and convex and g is continuous on U, then I(a, b) := integral_0^1 g(a + tau(b - a))(b - a) dtau is continuous on U x U.

0. The bad set. Let N0 := {p ∈ R^n : not (p ∈ U => f has Frechet derivative g(p) at p)}. Equivalently, N0 = {p ∈ U : f does not have derivative g(p) at p}. The hypothesis "for a.e. x, x ∈ U => HasFDerivAt f (g x) x" says exactly L^n(N0) = 0 (ae_iff). If p ∈ U and p ∉ N0, then f has derivative g(p) at p.

1. Setup. Fix x, y ∈ U and put h := y - x. U is open, so there are rho1, rho2 > 0 with B^o_rho1(x) ⊆ U and B^o_rho2(y) ⊆ U. Let rho := min(rho1, rho2) > 0. Then B^o_rho(x) ⊆ U and B^o_rho(y) ⊆ U. For every w ∈ B^o_rho(0), ||(x + w) - x|| = ||w|| < rho, so x + w ∈ U; likewise y + w ∈ U. Also, for a, b ∈ U and tau ∈ [0, 1], a + tau(b - a) = (1 - tau)a + tau b ∈ U by convexity.
Let I be as in [segment_integral_continuous], and define F(w) := f(y + w) - f(x + w) - I(x + w, y + w) for w ∈ R^n. Since F(0) = f(y) - f(x) - integral_0^1 g(x + tau(y - x))(y - x) dtau, the goal is F(0) = 0.

2. F vanishes at every good w. Claim: if w ∈ B^o_rho(0) and L^1({t ∈ R : x + w + t h ∈ N0}) = 0, then F(w) = 0.
Proof of the claim. Put sigma(t) := x + w + t h. Since (y + w) - (x + w) = h, sigma(t) = (x + w) + t((y + w) - (x + w)). As x + w and y + w lie in U, step 1 gives sigma(t) ∈ U for every t ∈ [0, 1].
 (a) phi(t) := f(sigma(t)) is (K||h||)-Lipschitz on [0, 1]. For t, t' ∈ [0, 1], both sigma(t) and sigma(t') lie in U, so
 ||phi(t) - phi(t')|| <= K||sigma(t) - sigma(t')|| = K||(t - t')h|| = K||h|| |t - t'|.
 (b) k(t) := g(sigma(t)) h is continuous on [0, 1]. g is continuous on U, sigma is continuous and maps [0, 1] into U, and evaluation at the fixed vector h is continuous (ContinuousOn.comp, ContinuousOn.clm_apply).
 (c) For a.e. t ∈ (0, 1), phi has derivative k(t) at t. The hypothesis L^1({t : sigma(t) ∈ N0}) = 0 means sigma(t) ∉ N0 for a.e. t (ae_iff). Take such a t with t ∈ (0, 1). Then sigma(t) ∈ U and sigma(t) ∉ N0, so f has Frechet derivative g(sigma(t)) at sigma(t) by step 0. The affine map sigma has derivative h at t: t |-> t h has derivative h, and adding a constant does not change it. By the chain rule (HasFDerivAt.comp_hasDerivAt), phi = f o sigma has derivative g(sigma(t)) h = k(t) at t.
 (d) Apply [lipschitz_ftc] with a = 0, b = 1, Lipschitz constant K||h||, the curve phi and the continuous function k. This gives phi(1) - phi(0) = integral_0^1 k(tau) dtau. Here phi(1) = f(x + w + h) = f(y + w) and phi(0) = f(x + w). Also
 integral_0^1 k(tau) dtau = integral_0^1 g(x + w + tau h) h dtau = integral_0^1 g((x + w) + tau((y + w) - (x + w)))((y + w) - (x + w)) dtau = I(x + w, y + w).
Hence f(y + w) - f(x + w) = I(x + w, y + w), that is, F(w) = 0.

3. F = 0 almost everywhere on B^o_rho(0). Apply [segment_null] to the null set N0, the point x and the direction h: for L^n-a.e. w, L^1({t : x + w + t h ∈ N0}) = 0. By step 2, for L^n-a.e. w: w ∈ B^o_rho(0) => F(w) = 0. The ball is measurable, so this says F = 0 almost everywhere for L^n restricted to B^o_rho(0) (ae_restrict_iff').

4. F is continuous on B^o_rho(0). f is continuous on U, because a map that is Lipschitz on U is continuous on U (LipschitzOnWith.continuousOn). The maps w |-> y + w and w |-> x + w are continuous and send B^o_rho(0) into U (step 1). So w |-> f(y + w) and w |-> f(x + w) are continuous on B^o_rho(0). By [segment_integral_continuous] (U open and convex, g continuous on U), I is continuous on U x U. The continuous map w |-> (x + w, y + w) sends B^o_rho(0) into U x U, so w |-> I(x + w, y + w) is continuous on B^o_rho(0). Differences of continuous maps are continuous, so F is continuous on B^o_rho(0).

5. F vanishes on the whole ball, in particular at 0. Let Z := {w ∈ B^o_rho(0) : F(w) ≠ 0}. Z is open, because F is continuous on the open ball and {v : v ≠ 0} is open. Z is L^n-null by step 3. Lebesgue measure gives positive measure to every nonempty open set, so Z is empty. In Lean this is Measure.eqOn_open_of_ae_eq, applied to the open ball, the continuous maps F and 0, and Lebesgue measure (an IsOpenPosMeasure). Since rho > 0, 0 ∈ B^o_rho(0), so F(0) = 0, that is,
 f(y) - f(x) = I(x, y) = integral_0^1 g(x + tau(y - x))(y - x) dtau.
Since x and y were arbitrary points of U, the formula holds for all x, y ∈ U.
proof_key_steps: N0 := {p ∈ U : not HasFDerivAt f (g p) p} is L^n-null (ae_iff)
Fix x, y ∈ U, h = y - x and rho > 0 with B_rho(x), B_rho(y) ⊆ U; define F(w) := f(y + w) - f(x + w) - I(x + w, y + w)
If w ∈ B_rho(0) and its segment meets N0 in an L^1-null set: t |-> f(x + w + t h) is K||h||-Lipschitz on [0,1] with a.e. derivative g(x + w + t h)h (chain rule), so lipschitz_ftc gives F(w) = 0
segment_null: F = 0 a.e. on B_rho(0)
F is continuous on B_rho(0) (f Lipschitz; segment_integral_continuous); a continuous function that is a.e. zero on an open set vanishes there (Measure.eqOn_open_of_ae_eq), so F(0) = 0

subproblems.title: Frechet differentiability from the integral mean-value formula
subproblems.statement: Let n, l >= 0, f : R^n -> R^l, g : R^n -> L(R^n, R^l), U ⊆ R^n open and x ∈ U. Suppose g is continuous on U and f(y) - f(x) = integral_0^1 g(x + tau(y - x))(y - x) dtau for every y ∈ U. Then f has Frechet derivative g(x) at x.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (n ℓ : ℕ) (f : Rn n → Rn ℓ) (g : Rn n → (Rn n →L[ℝ] Rn ℓ)) (U : Set (Rn n)) (x : Rn n), IsOpen U → x ∈ U → ContinuousOn g U → (∀ y ∈ U, f y - f x = ∫ τ in (0:ℝ)..1, g (x + τ • (y - x)) (y - x)) → HasFDerivAt f (g x) x
subproblems.natural_proof:
This is step 4 of the parent proof.

1. Reformulation. By hasFDerivAt_iff_isLittleO_nhds_zero and Asymptotics.isLittleO_iff, it suffices to show: for every epsilon > 0 there is a neighbourhood of 0 in R^n on which ||f(x + h) - f(x) - g(x)h|| <= epsilon||h||.

2. Choice of eta. Fix epsilon > 0. U is open and x ∈ U, so g is continuous at x (ContinuousOn.continuousAt with IsOpen.mem_nhds). Since U is open, choose eta1 > 0 with B^o_eta1(x) ⊆ U. By continuity at x, choose eta2 > 0 with ||g(z) - g(x)|| < epsilon whenever ||z - x|| < eta2. Let eta := min(eta1, eta2) > 0. Then B^o_eta(x) ⊆ U and ||g(z) - g(x)|| <= epsilon for all z ∈ B^o_eta(x).

3. The segment stays in the ball. Let h ∈ B^o_eta(0), i.e. ||h|| < eta; this set is a neighbourhood of 0. For tau ∈ [0, 1], ||(x + tau h) - x|| = tau||h|| <= ||h|| < eta, so x + tau h ∈ B^o_eta(x) ⊆ U. In particular y := x + h ∈ U and y - x = h, so the hypothesis gives
 f(x + h) - f(x) = integral_0^1 g(x + tau h) h dtau.

4. Rewriting the remainder. The function tau |-> g(x + tau h) h is continuous on [0, 1]: g is continuous on U, tau |-> x + tau h is continuous with values in U (step 3), and evaluation at h is continuous. So it is interval integrable on 0..1. The constant g(x)h is interval integrable, and integral_0^1 g(x)h dtau = g(x)h. By linearity of the integral (intervalIntegral.integral_sub),
 f(x + h) - f(x) - g(x)h = integral_0^1 (g(x + tau h)h - g(x)h) dtau.

5. Estimate. For tau ∈ (0, 1] (the set Ι 0 1) we have x + tau h ∈ B^o_eta(x). By ContinuousLinearMap.le_opNorm,
 ||g(x + tau h)h - g(x)h|| = ||(g(x + tau h) - g(x))h|| <= ||g(x + tau h) - g(x)|| ||h|| <= epsilon||h||.
By intervalIntegral.norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const,
 ||integral_0^1 (g(x + tau h)h - g(x)h) dtau|| <= epsilon||h|| |1 - 0| = epsilon||h||.

6. Conclusion. For all h with ||h|| < eta, ||f(x + h) - f(x) - g(x)h|| <= epsilon||h||. Since epsilon > 0 was arbitrary, f(x + h) - f(x) - g(x)h = o(||h||) as h -> 0. That is, f has Frechet derivative g(x) at x.
proof_key_steps: Reduce to: for each epsilon > 0, eventually ||f(x+h) - f(x) - g(x)h|| <= epsilon||h|| (hasFDerivAt_iff_isLittleO_nhds_zero, Asymptotics.isLittleO_iff)
Choose eta > 0 with B_eta(x) ⊆ U and ||g(z) - g(x)|| <= epsilon on B_eta(x)
For ||h|| < eta, apply the hypothesis with y = x + h; the remainder equals integral_0^1 (g(x + tau h) - g(x))h dtau (integrability from continuity)
The norm of that integral is at most epsilon||h|| (norm_integral_le_of_norm_le_const)
